paragraphs: The US launched limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island late on Monday, according to reports in US media, hours after Vice President JD Vance said he was optimistic that diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction. The Wall Street Journal first reported the strikes. Reuters and the Associated Press reported that they targeted surface-to-air missiles being used against US assets.

The strikes were reported as "defensive" and were not thought to signal a return to full hostilities, The Guardian said. Iranian state media reported several explosions on the island on Monday evening, while local outlets described the cause as unclear. US Central Command did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The Journal said the attacks were part of a series carried out in recent weeks that have not been made public. It reported that they were smaller in scale and deliberately kept secret by the Trump administration so as not to signal an intent to resume the military campaign. If confirmed, this would be the first publicly known US strike on Iran in weeks.

Qeshm sits at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz and has been used in the past to launch attacks on shipping. Although attacks have ceased in recent weeks, Iran has continued to enforce its closure of the strait by targeting tankers and other vessels, according to The Guardian.

Vance told reporters he and President Trump "feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement," after Tehran revealed indirect negotiations with Washington. Asked earlier whether he had considered resuming strikes after Tuesday's midterms, Trump said "no." Speaking to Fox News, he said "there's no war raging," but added the US might still "have to go after Pickaxe mountain," a fortified underground site in central Iran that is a suspected nuclear facility. He said that would take about an hour. Iran's response to the reported strikes was not included in the source text.

Americans are voting in midterm elections that will determine control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, both currently held by Republicans. All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are on the ballot, according to Al Jazeera. The Guardian described the contest as widely seen as a referendum on Donald Trump's second term.

Opinion surveys suggest Democrats are well positioned to win the House, The Guardian reported, while the Senate is a tougher task. A final New York Times and Siena University set of polls published Sunday put Democratic candidates ahead in five of seven key battleground contests, including Texas and Kansas. Trump's approval ratings are reported at between 33 and 37 percent. Democrats are emphasizing affordability, alleged corruption and the effect of the Iran war on living costs.

Both parties faced late turmoil. In Michigan, Democratic Representative Haley Stevens, who lost her party's Senate primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers; Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called the move "a despicable betrayal." In Alaska, a report said the Democratic candidate's campaign was behind an effort to recruit a challenger with nearly the same name as Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. Candidate Mary Peltola denied any knowledge of such a scheme. The Justice Department also sued to block certification of Alaska's results; a judge dismissed the suit. Opponents say some Justice Department actions are meant to cast doubt on the election, and critics have denounced a planned record 1,000 election monitors as intimidation. The administration's response to those criticisms was not given in the source text.

Polls close from 6pm Eastern, starting in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. Al Jazeera said many races could be called Tuesday night, but close contests could take days. Alaska and Maine use ranked-choice voting, and California, Arizona, Nevada and Washington may count mail ballots slowly.

The US Supreme Court on Monday denied a Trump administration request tied to about 20,000 California ballots, ending its bid before Election Day. The Justice Department wanted ballots set aside from registered voters it describes as likely noncitizens. The court's one-line order denied the department's application for an injunction pending appeal. Fox News reported that Justice Elena Kagan denied it without comment; the BBC said the application was referred by her to the full court.

The department argued that once illegally cast ballots are counted and mixed with lawful votes, the harm is impossible to remedy. It said its request would preserve ballots during an investigation without canceling votes. California and Los Angeles County disputed the federal list's accuracy and said segregating ballots while voting is under way is infeasible. NPR reported that UCLA data scientists granted access to the list by a court order in another case found 42 percent of names do not appear on California's current voter roll, and that it included naturalized citizens.

A federal judge in Los Angeles, David Carter, and a divided 9th Circuit panel had already rejected the request. The majority cited the principle that election rules should not change on the eve of an election, state authority over elections and a federal ban on systematic voter removals within 90 days of an election. Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented.

Separately, Fox News reported that Chief Judge James Boasberg in Washington said it was "likely" the administration violated the Constitution and issued an injunction against its requests to California over mail ballots. NPR reported a San Francisco judge's temporary restraining order, which the government has appealed. The Justice Department has also sent subpoenas to California election officials.

A federal magistrate judge on Monday dismissed the Justice Department's criminal case against two former FBI officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides. They were charged about two weeks ago with lying to Congress in 2023 about their knowledge of FBI investigations involving Hunter Biden. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui ruled from the bench in Washington after a days-long preliminary hearing on whether probable cause existed.

Faruqui said he was "deeply troubled" and that what happened "cannot be described as anything other than weaponization." According to NPR, he described the investigation as rushed and error-ridden and noted it was opened on FBI Director Kash Patel's orders the day after a Trump primetime address urging the FBI to investigate. He also noted the alleged statements dated to 2023, the department waited three years, and charges came about two weeks before the midterms despite a department policy against timing actions to influence an election. Fox News said he described the case as a "rush job" directed by Trump and Patel, and that he struck a revised complaint that sought to add obstruction charges without judicial approval.

The Justice Department said it disagrees with the decision, which it said appears to suggest high-ranking officials are immune from accountability for materially false statements to Congress. It said it is evaluating all options. Fox News noted Republicans have long accused the FBI of improperly handling information about Hunter Biden before the 2020 election, and that prosecutors alleged the officials' statements were contradicted by internal communications and witnesses. Floris's attorney, Margaret Donovan, said the government had no case.

The dismissal does not bar prosecutors from seeking a grand jury indictment, Faruqui said, and they could also appeal to the district's chief judge. Fox News said it asked the White House and FBI for comment.

Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre and a neighbouring shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha in southern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region on Monday. Ukrainian officials said at least 26 people were killed. The BBC later reported that regional head Mykhailo Semikin put the toll at 29 on Tuesday, with search and rescue still under way.

According to the BBC, 10 people were injured and 48 were reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs struck. Emergency services said two rescuers and four police officers were among the dead. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russian forces first hit a school used for humanitarian needs just as people were arriving, then struck the shelter. He called it a "vile terrorist strike" and said residents gathered there weekly for aid. Rescue work was repeatedly halted by Russian drone attacks, officials said. A day of mourning was declared across the region for Tuesday. The Russian military has not publicly commented, the BBC said.

Zelensky argued the attack showed Russia does not want de-escalation. He pointed to a recent evacuation of civilians from Russian-occupied Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, the longest pause in fighting in the war. The Kremlin said, according to The Guardian, that no similar missions were planned "at the moment."

US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine are due to resume on November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi, US envoy Steve Witkoff said. The BBC said no major breakthrough is expected, and Witkoff said the agenda includes post-war security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian efforts. He added that US negotiators would meet European and NATO officials in Brussels this week.

Palantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates on Monday, and for the first time its US commercial revenue exceeded its US government revenue, CNBC reported. Shares dipped about 3 percent in extended trading.

US commercial revenue jumped 148 percent to $984 million, compared with US government revenue of $953 million, which rose 96 percent. Palantir said US commercial revenue has more than quintupled over the last two years. Overall revenue nearly doubled from a year earlier and passed $2 billion for the first time. Net income more than doubled to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents per share, from about $476 million, or 18 cents per share.

The company raised its outlook. It now expects full-year US commercial revenue "in excess of" $3.56 billion, up from a forecast of $3.42 billion last quarter. It projects about $2.65 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and about $8.53 billion for full-year 2026.

CEO Alex Karp told CNBC that "I don't believe anyone's had consistent results like this in the history of software AI, ever," and said the business is succeeding without salespeople. CNBC noted that Palantir has long been known for its strength in government work, and that businesses are adopting more of its artificial intelligence tools.

Karp has supported open-weight models and criticized leading AI labs, saying they force businesses to give up data sovereignty, CNBC reported. On Monday he repeated calls to nationalize AI labs, calling it the "only realistic way" to manage liability. He also said, "Beware of thinking you can delay the future in AI."

Anthropic filed an amended Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors updated financials as it moves toward a potential initial public offering, CNBC reported. The initial prospectus, released last week, covered only the first half of the year.

The company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended September 30, up roughly 1,200 percent from a year earlier. It reported a $104 billion net loss for the period, though CNBC said most of that stemmed from changes in the fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. The loss over the same stretch in 2025 was $25.1 billion.

Third-quarter revenue was roughly $17 billion, up about 1,127 percent from a year earlier, with a net loss of $23.29 billion. Growth slowed from the prior quarter: revenue rose around 47 percent in the third quarter, compared with 144 percent growth in the second quarter and 132 percent in the first.

Anthropic said it has purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure." Its compute and infrastructure expenses rose by $14.4 billion for the nine months, up 329 percent.

CNBC said the company faces market jitters about the AI buildout, with Wall Street worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for data center developers. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX and some from neoclouds. Its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors. CNBC also reported that rival OpenAI confidentially filed in June, though its executives have signaled a 2027 debut.
Israeli forces killed at least four Palestinians in Gaza on Monday, and a fifth person died of wounds from an earlier attack, according to medical sources and media reports cited by Al Jazeera.

Medical sources said at least two people were killed in a gun attack and an air raid in southern Khan Younis, and a third in a drone attack in the central village of al-Musaddar. The Wafa news agency said a fourth person, identified as Hani Hamed Kahil, was killed in a strike on a vehicle in the Tal al-Hawa area of northern Gaza City, with five others wounded. Wafa also reported that Youssef Abu Younis died of injuries from an Israeli attack on a police post in al-Mawasi on Sunday.

The Israeli military said it targeted Palestinian fighters in three strikes but gave no further details. Al Jazeera also reported that at least five police officers were killed on Sunday, and that three people were wounded in Gaza City when a community kitchen's minibus was hit.

The Palestinian Ministry of Health says Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,593 Palestinians and wounded 5,748 since the US-brokered ceasefire began in October 2025. Al Jazeera's weekly roundup said the UN human rights office warned on October 30 that Palestinians are being pushed into an ever smaller area, describing the "Yellow Line" as a "kill zone" moving westward.

Shelter is a pressing concern before winter. Israeli Army Radio reported that Nickolay Mladenov, high representative of the US-established Board of Peace, arrived in Israel on Monday to seek permission to bring in tents and to push for faster reconstruction. The UN migration agency said on October 9 that nearly two million people needed shelter assistance and that half of Gaza's tents and makeshift shelters needed replacing.

The German government is warning politicians and public figures that they may have been targeted by government-backed spyware, days after Apple began sending notifications saying their iPhones may have been hacked, according to TechCrunch.

Germany's federal cybersecurity office, the BSI, said in a note over the weekend that members of the Bundestag and other unnamed notable individuals had received the warnings. Citing the Financial Times, TechCrunch reported that government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin was taking the incident and the warning very seriously. He did not say who in the federal government had been targeted, including whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among them.

Apple periodically notifies people it believes may have been targeted by spyware, which can steal messages, location data and other sensitive information. Such tools often use zero-click exploits that require no action from the victim. Apple does not blame specific governments or say whether a phone was actually compromised, so the BSI advised that anyone who receives such a notification should assume the device may have been compromised.

The alerts reached people beyond Germany. Beirut-based filmmaker Radwan Mortada said on X that he received a notice warning of "another attack against your device," after being targeted by spyware in 2021. According to that notice, Apple's latest batch went to users in 99 countries.

It is unclear who is behind this round of attacks or which government may have orchestrated it. TechCrunch noted that governments often buy such tools from private vendors, including Israel's NSO Group, maker of Pegasus, and that Germany's federal criminal police office, the BKA, reportedly bought access to Pegasus in 2019.

Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor into 1.3 million devices and used it to create a botnet, according to The Verge. The company says it has dismantled the backdoor and cut ties with the manufacturer, Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology Co.

Google said Videostrong has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices, and from supplying software for them. It said the infected devices were used without their owners' knowledge for malicious activity such as ad fraud, data exfiltration and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed and operated for financial gain.

According to Google, Videostrong made money by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates' malware modules onto infected devices. The company said those modules carried out ad fraud, quietly enrolled devices in residential proxy networks, and loaded additional malware onto devices compromised through the backdoor, which it called XCPE.

Google said it also acted to disrupt the command and control domains that run the affiliate modules. Because the affiliates distribute their modules through other channels as well, Google assessed that taking down those domains will cut access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

The malware was found built into many device models and brands over several years. Most were Android TV set-top boxes, but Google said the botnet also affected other Android-based internet-connected devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signage. Google said Videostrong used obfuscation techniques to load the malware after users first booted the hardware, and that it has changed its review process for device manufacturers following the incident.

U.S. officials suspect Iran-linked hackers are behind a series of cyberattacks that caused freezers at military bases around the country to malfunction, according to Defense One, which cited two people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The outages have affected around six commissaries, the on-base grocery stores serving military personnel, and began around late August. It is not clear how the intruders gained access to the freezer systems, though Defense One said various digital vulnerabilities tied to freezer controls can expose such equipment to hacking and sabotage. The assessment could change as investigators learn more.

Defense One said that, if the link to Iran is fully confirmed, the attacks would show Tehran's ability to disrupt military-related equipment inside the United States through cyber means. The report noted that the Trump administration is reportedly planning follow-up strikes on Iran after next week's midterm elections. It also said Tehran is suspected of backing recent attacks on U.S. water-treatment equipment, which would fit a broader pattern of suspected Iranian activity in recent months.

Cyber Command and Defense Department law enforcement units are investigating, and French authorities are working with them. Earlier this month, hackers overrode temperature controls on commercial refrigeration equipment at about 350 French establishments, forcing supermarkets to discard spoiled food.

The Food and Agriculture Information Sharing and Analysis Center, an industry group, has warned that attackers can target internet-accessible industrial controls that may lack strong cyberdefenses. Defense One said the case draws attention to an often overlooked area of cybersecurity: computers that control everyday food storage and handling equipment.
OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company, CNBC reports.

OpenAI said Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity. He will work with the company's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular emphasis on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly. His updated LinkedIn profile also lists the new position.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the United States has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology. Driscoll said "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," adding that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to people working in national security.

CNBC said the appointment follows Driscoll's departure as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed to modernize the U.S. military, including by expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous Army announcement. He also met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from Ukraine's Presidential Office.

At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's cyber resilience efforts through its Daybreak program.

Chinese space officials confirmed this weekend that China plans to land astronauts on the Moon within three years, according to Ars Technica. At a manned spaceflight conference in Beijing, officials including Wang Xiang, chief designer for the lunar exploration program, laid out the most detailed public plan yet for missions leading to a crewed landing "before 2030."

Based on slides shared on social media, the plan begins with an uncrewed test of the Long March 10A rocket and the Mengzhou spacecraft in low-Earth orbit, targeted for early 2027. An uncrewed test of the larger Long March 10 and the Lanyue lunar lander, including descent and ascent from the Moon, is targeted for 2028. In 2029, two Long March 10 rockets would launch together, one carrying an uncrewed Mengzhou and the other Lanyue, and dock in lunar orbit. The crewed landing mission would follow, with the same dual-launch design.

Because China lacks a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V, the crew and lander will launch separately. Ars Technica noted the plan omits, for now, a crewed flyby or orbit mission like Apollo 8 or Artemis II.

NASA has set a target of landing humans on the Moon by 2028, about a year ahead of China. Ars Technica said questions remain over the lunar landers being developed by SpaceX and Blue Origin, and a U.S. landing could slip to 2030 or later depending on their progress.

It said China is making credible progress, citing an August 2025 test of a Lanyue mock-up and the arrival of the 2027 Mengzhou spacecraft at the Wenchang launch site. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has streamlined Artemis and committed to a lunar surface base over the next decade.

Shareholders of Churchill Capital Corp XI have approved the special purpose acquisition company's proposed business combination with humanoid robot developer Agility Robotics, moving Agility closer to becoming a publicly traded company, The Robot Report says.

More than 84% of votes cast at a special meeting on Nov. 2 supported the deal. The transaction is expected to close on Nov. 4, with the combined company due to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Nov. 5 under the ticker AGLT. Churchill Capital stock finished up nearly 14% on Nov. 2.

The deal is expected to provide Agility about $465 million in gross capital before expenses, down from more than $620 million anticipated when it was announced in June. That total includes about $164 million from Churchill's trust account, about $201 million from a Foxconn-led private investment in public equity, and $100 million Agility received after the initial announcement. The original deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion pre-money, and existing shareholders will roll their equity into the combined company.

Agility's Digit robots are operating in nine customer environments, mainly in logistics and manufacturing. It has worked with GXO Logistics since 2023 and, in October, announced expansion to two more GXO facilities, with deployments expected to begin in early 2027. Agricultural equipment maker AGCO also signed an agreement to pilot Digit at a Kansas plant starting in 2027.

The company has said it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for its next-generation Digit 5. The Robot Report cautioned that this figure should not be confused with current revenue, as it remains subject to contractual milestones and product specifications.

Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, is reportedly pushing the company's development of household robots, and the first to debut may be a roaming home robot, according to Ars Technica, which cited a report from The Information based on people who worked on the projects.

The robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra, in line with Apple's new HomeView stationary smart display. It would autonomously move around a home, support FaceTime calls and turn lights on when a person enters a room. Apple is reportedly aiming for a launch by 2027 at a price of $1,000 or more, although development delays could push it to 2028.

Prototypes first appeared in 2018, with approval from former CEO Tim Cook to continue. The Information said engineers are trying to give the robot capabilities beyond being a "fancy way to make FaceTime calls" to justify a high price. One source described a very small team of about 10 "true roboticists," many original members having left, alongside roughly 300 people on software.

Ternus is also reportedly backing a separate project on robots for household tasks such as folding clothes. That would presumably need robotic arms, though it is unclear whether Apple intends a general-purpose humanoid like those from startups 1X and Figure AI.

Ars Technica said the robot's few reported features seem underwhelming next to existing smart home devices, and questioned whether enough customers would pay more than $1,000 for it. It also said a limited-purpose robot makes more sense for now, on technical and safety grounds, than a general-purpose one.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democrat, has threatened to sue the Trump administration over Immigration and Customs Enforcement's reported use of city-owned parking lots to stage immigration enforcement operations, Fox News reports.

In a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella and ICE New York field office Director Kenneth Genalo, Mamdani said he was "deeply troubled" by reports of agents using city property to stage operations. He wrote that the use is unauthorized and illegal, and that if it continues "New York City will take legal action to prevent this unlawful commandeering of City property."

According to the letter, agents have reportedly parked vehicles and held meetings in several unstaffed city lots, including one at Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx and lots along 111th Street at Flushing Meadows Corona Park in Queens. The mayor noted the Queens lots are next to a city-run preschool and cultural institutions. He said ICE has not sought authorization and demanded that it immediately issue guidance barring agents from using city lots for enforcement.
Fox News said it had asked the Department of Homeland Security for comment. The agency's response to this letter was not included in the report.

Last month, Mamdani and other Democratic leaders asked private parking lot owners not to rent or lend property to ICE as a staging area. More than 100 elected officials signed that letter, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. Fox News noted Mamdani has previously called for ICE to be abolished.

Anthropic has warned in a revised S-1/A filing, submitted Monday, that it may soon reach what it calls recursive self-improvement, according to TechCrunch. The outlet describes the concept, known as RSI, as the point at which AI becomes so good at training itself that AI capabilities accelerate dramatically.

In new language in its Risk Factors section, Anthropic said its growing use of AI to speed up its own research and development "may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures." It said it has in the past not identified, and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration until after it has occurred.

The filing said internal estimates and expectations for future models, rather than current ones, indicate the company "may imminently meet" its Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of "dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI." Anthropic said it has not designated any current model as exceeding that threshold and is still assessing the underlying data.

Anthropic also said it does not expect to be able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding. It said it is considering updates to its policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development.

TechCrunch notes that people who fear advanced AI see RSI as a point of no return, in which AI could slip beyond human control, while enthusiasts see a tool for productivity and scientific discovery. The article adds that skeptics may say an S-1 works as both disclosure and marketing, and that Claude's coding, math and cybersecurity abilities have grown quickly this year.

The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, the highest level since November 2008. CNBC said the move matched expectations in a Reuters poll of economists and was the bank's fifth increase this year. The decision was split: six board members voted for a rise and three for no change.

Governor Michele Bullock told reporters inflation is "too high" and forecast to stay higher for longer. "Some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track," she said. Consumer prices rose 4.3% in September, up from 4% in August. The Guardian reported the bank's forecasts show inflation near 4.5% by the end of 2026 and returning to its 2 to 3% target range only by the end of next year.

The Guardian said the RBA's statement dropped an explicit reference to further hikes, which UBS economists called "clearly dovish". Markets halved the odds of another rise before Christmas to 12%, but still priced roughly a 30% chance of a sixth hike by May. An EY economist said a wait-and-see approach over summer was likely, though more increases could not be ruled out.

Politicians offered differing explanations. Treasurer Jim Chalmers said higher fuel prices from the Middle East conflict were the "primary driver" of inflation and that government budgets are not adding to it. Opposition leader Angus Taylor said "Labor's spending spree is driving up inflation" and interest rates.

Canstar estimated the latest rise adds $107 a month to repayments on a $700,000 loan. The RBA forecasts weak growth, with unemployment, now 4.7%, reaching about 4.9% by the end of next year. Bullock said recession is not the bank's base case.

North Korea has denied involvement in the $6.3 billion hack of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric", the BBC reports. Kim Yo Jong, a senior official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said Tuesday the accusations were a "sinister attempt" by the United States to damage Pyongyang's public image.

The FBI, the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the attack, which has been described as the largest hack in history. Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said it was led by the state-backed group TraderTraitor, also known as the Lazarus Group. The FBI has asked industry partners to help block transactions involving crypto accounts linked to the group.

In her statement, Kim Yo Jong said the US was "misleading the international public opinion" by implying that all cybercrimes around the world are North Korea's doing. She said opposing malicious acts in cyberspace is the government's consistent policy. The BBC notes that North Korea has been blamed for several major cyber attacks in recent years and has denied them all, including a then-record $1.5 billion hack of the exchange Bybit in 2025 that was attributed to the same unit.

Research groups such as the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies say North Korea has built up its cyber operations by recruiting university students into hacker units overseen by its intelligence agency. North Korea has consistently denied such claims.

Binance has focused on the technical side. It said last week that initial checks indicated an engineer's laptop was compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals. Trading in major cryptocurrencies has resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze affected assets. Binance said a net $5.27 billion has been withdrawn since Sunday, that activity has stabilised, and that it has covered about 95% of the stolen assets.

A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, the state's first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced Monday. Governor Kathy Hochul said the child died in Lewis County, about 93 miles north of Syracuse, and that she was "heartbroken" by the news.

Hochul tied the death to federal vaccine policy. She called it "a devastating reminder of what's at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses." The Guardian noted that Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has faced criticism over comments on some vaccines and has made sweeping changes to vaccination policy, including cutting childhood immunisation recommendations by a third. A response from the department to Hochul's statement was not included in the report.

The Guardian said measles is highly contagious and, though rare, causes death in roughly one to three of every 1,000 cases. The US stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by keeping vaccination rates high, but rates have fallen below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.

The CDC had confirmed three measles-associated deaths nationwide this year, though state health departments have reported more. Pennsylvania officials have reported six. As of late October the CDC counted 4,588 cases in 2026, more than double the 2025 total. Pennsylvania accounted for 1,338 of them, and South Carolina and Utah each reported more than 500.

Hochul declared a disaster emergency in early October because of measles cases in neighbouring states and in rural parts of New York. Her order widened the pool of people who can give measles vaccines to include paramedics and midwives, and let nurses order testing.

A Yakima County, Washington, resident has died of complications from bird flu after exposure at a dairy with infected cattle, county health officials said. The person, who had underlying health conditions, had been hospitalized and died Sunday. Officials did not release further details, citing the family's privacy. The CDC said the person was infected with H5N1.

STAT, citing the Associated Press, reported this is the first US bird flu death in a year. Ars Technica described it as the third since the virus made the jump from wild birds to dairy cows, first reported in the US in March 2024. The earlier deaths were a Louisiana resident in January 2025 and a Washington resident in November 2025, who was infected with a rarer H5N5 version.

County officials reported that 33 dairy herds have recently tested positive for H5N1 and that three human infections have been linked to dairy exposure. The Yakima Health District is working with the state to find and monitor close contacts. Ars Technica said the other two people did not become severely ill or require hospitalization. The USDA reports 40 detections in Washington dairy cows since October 8 and 134 cattle cases nationally this year.

Health officials say the risk to the public remains low. Dave Atteberry, the Yakima health officer, said the virus can cause severe illness, particularly in people with underlying conditions. A CDC spokesperson said genetic analysis of the virus found no changes that would make it spread more easily or cause more severe illness. More than 70 human cases have been reported since 2024 with no known person-to-person spread.
Ars Technica also pointed to a report of the virus on a Utah mink farm, which it said raised concern because mink could give the virus chances to mutate.

The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal to remove post-Brexit checks on food and agriculture exports, ahead of a UK-EU summit later this month, the BBC reports. The BBC understands the 200-page text has been circulated to EU nations for discussion at a meeting of ambassadors on Wednesday. Draft texts on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme, plus a 15-page joint statement for leaders, were circulated too.

The BBC calls the food agreement the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset so far. It should end the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, £25 Phytosanitary certificates, inspector fees and some port and sampling fees. UK exports of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would resume, and UK pets could get passports for EU travel. The government claims eventual annual benefits of £5.1bn.

In return, the UK would commit to "dynamic alignment", meaning it would follow and adapt to existing EU rules on plant, animal and food standards. The government has announced a European Partnerships Bill to provide a legal mechanism for applying new EU rules. Linking the two emissions trading schemes would also spare UK exporters the EU's carbon border tax.

Supermarkets and farmers' representatives back the food plans, the BBC says, while some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised reapplying EU rules. Details of youth scheme numbers are still to be settled politically, and discounted student fees for EU students and a plan to reconnect electricity markets are likely to be pushed to next year.

Separately, the British Chambers of Commerce said the current relationship is "failing to deliver" and urged the government to examine nine options, including a customs union. The prime minister has said he wants the summit to launch a conversation on a longer-term path, including rejoining the bloc.

President Donald Trump has told Congress he intends to remove South Africa and Rwanda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act, known as Agoa, from 1 January 2027, the BBC reports. The programme lets eligible African countries export thousands of products to the US duty-free.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said an annual review found both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements. The administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, and concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region. For Rwanda it also raised human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights. For South Africa it additionally pointed to corruption. Greer said the administration is working to ensure African partners "take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria."

The move came about a week after the US Treasury sanctioned Rwanda's defence ministry. The Treasury said the ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo and supplied weapons, equipment, logistics and training. The BBC did not report a Rwandan response.

South Africa's trade minister, Parks Tau, called the decision "unfortunate" and said Washington was raising new issues that had not featured in trade talks that began in 2025. He said South Africa will accelerate the diversification of its export markets to protect jobs. US Ambassador Leo Brent Bozell III said on X that the outcome was "predictable and preventable" and resulted from the South African government rejecting real US concerns.

The BBC notes relations with both countries are strained. Last year Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.

Australia's High Court on Tuesday began hearing the first major legal challenge to the country's under-16 social media ban, which took effect in December last year. The challenge was brought by Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project, a group led by New South Wales Libertarian MP John Ruddick. Reddit argues the law impinges the implied freedom of political communication for under-16s.

Reddit's counsel, Perry Herzfeld, told the court the law was passed within a week of being announced in 2024, with only 24 hours for submissions, which he said was likely to produce "ill-thought-out, over-broad legislation." He said the ban prevents teenagers from posting, commenting or upvoting on forums such as r/Australia, though they can still view content without an account. Reddit pointed to alternatives such as a digital duty of care bill before parliament, limits on push notifications or time spent, and parental controls. In written submissions, Reddit also said the ban's effectiveness has been limited and that there is no scientific consensus on the harms.
Justice Jacqueline Gleeson noted that the vast majority of teens, most of the time, do not engage in politics before 16.

Government barrister Joanna Davidson told the court that design features such as autoplay, recommendations and default notifications, which she said maximise engagement, are broadly shared across all 10 covered platforms, including Reddit. She said they can compound the risk of harms such as poor sleep and depression, and that children are more vulnerable. Communications Minister Anika Wells said the government's arguments would be made in court.

More than 5 million accounts believed to belong to under-16s have been suspended or deactivated since the ban began. The government is due to continue its argument on Wednesday. The Guardian said Reddit and the government disagree on whether the ban's limits on political communication are justified by a credible risk of harm.

Swedish manufacturer Saab has unveiled a suite of in-house AI agents designed for future aircraft platforms, after testing the technology on a Gripen E multirole fighter jet, according to Breaking Defense. A company statement said the move shows Saab's ability to develop, train and fly its own AI for air combat.

Saab said the agents use various AI techniques to master tactical decision-making in complex operational environments. They can work with a pilot in a cockpit or from their own uncrewed air vehicle. Central to the project is Saab's AI Fighter Jet Pilot Academy, which is meant to develop the agents and build the infrastructure needed to create, train and evaluate them.

Peter Nilsson, head of Advanced Programs at Saab's aeronautics unit, told Breaking Defense and other media that the harder question is how to turn the success of flying with the agents into a dependable capability that can keep learning and stay relevant. He called that the true purpose of the academy.

So far the agents have mostly been tested with the jet under beyond-visual-range combat conditions. Breaking Defense noted a similar 2025 campaign in which Helsing's Centaur AI tool took control of a Gripen and autonomously completed several such maneuvers. Longer term, Saab plans to use the technology in future air programs. The outlet previously reported that the company is developing three unmanned aircraft, the A1, A2 and A3, on the path toward a new loyal wingman drone.

To scale computing capacity, Saab has become a partial founder of Sferical AI, a Swedish government-backed initiative inaugurated in Stockholm last month. Nilsson said that otherwise Saab would have to pay companies such as Google or Amazon and might not have full control of its data. According to a Saab slide, Sferical AI is built on Nvidia's DGX SuperPOD architecture.

A Kyiv equipment maker called CODE380 is drawing attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D-Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen, according to TechCrunch and Defense News. The makers announced the device this month.

Many of these drones send video over the air without encryption, so a receiver tuned to the right frequency can show a Ukrainian unit where an attack is heading and what the pilot is aiming at before impact. The device uses a software-defined radio to sweep frequencies from 500 megahertz to 8.7 gigahertz, which the developers told the Ukrainian outlet DOU leaves no blind spots. Manufacturer figures reported by Militarnyi put its analog video range at up to 6 miles on lower frequencies and 2 to 3 miles on higher ones.

At roughly 10 ounces, Defense News reports, it weighs less than half as much as its main Ukrainian rivals. Those include Babai's Vydun 7.5 at about 2 pounds, Contra-drone's SENSE-4 at 21 ounces and BlueBird Tech's Chuyka 3.0 at up to 23 ounces, according to their manufacturers.

The receiver also covers the band where Russia's Molniya strike drones began sending video in June. Serhii Beskrestnov, a radio specialist and presidential adviser, wrote that most detectors do not see those frequencies, or see them poorly.

The advantage may not last. Beskrestnov has warned that digital video could one day fully replace analog, which would make portable detectors and fixed analog receiving stations ineffective. Defense News notes that many receivers already struggle with digital video and fiber-optic drones. TechCrunch adds that the New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, use Nvidia chips and emit no signals.

One patient in a small trial of a personalized mRNA pancreatic cancer vaccine shows no evidence of the disease years later, NPR reported. Donna Gustafson, a 72-year-old retired accountant, became the first person to receive such a vaccine seven years ago. She told NPR she now has full quality of life.

The vaccine was designed from samples of her tumor. It aims to train her immune cells to recognize distinctive mutant proteins on cancer cells and kill them. NPR said mRNA, genomics and AI were combined to create these vaccines, which are also being tested against lung, kidney, bladder and brain cancers.

Gustafson was one of 16 patients in the trial. She received nine doses along with surgery and chemotherapy. According to NPR, the vaccine worked in eight patients, seven of whom are still alive. She said she had no side effects. Surgeon and scientist Vinod Balachandran, who ran the trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, said her immune cells expanded ten-thousand-fold and stayed high years after her last shot, which he said shows the response lasts.

The result is one patient in a very small study, and NPR noted that researchers do not yet understand why some trials of these vaccines have failed while others show striking results. NPR also reported that Merck and Moderna recently released results from the first major successful trial of mRNA vaccines for skin cancer, which showed big reductions in recurrence and death.

The National Cancer Institute is working on a partnership with private companies to speed up development of more mRNA cancer vaccines, NPR said. Sloan Kettering plans to expand on-site manufacture of personalized vaccines for patients next year.

BMW says it will expand its navigation-guided, partially automated driving into city streets starting in 2027, launching first in Germany with other markets to follow, The Verge reports. The feature will arrive on select models through software updates and is aimed at rivaling Tesla's Full Self-Driving.

According to the report, the system can help steer, speed up and slow down on highways and city streets using the car's built-in GPS navigation. In town it can assist with lane changes, turns, yielding to other cars and roundabouts. It is a Level 2 system, so drivers must watch the road and be ready to take over. On highways BMW will allow hands off the wheel, but on local roads drivers must keep their hands on it.

BMW says the system works cooperatively with drivers, who can steer, brake or accelerate without switching it off. The car shows what it sees and what the system is doing on the heads-up display and a 3D map on the main screen.

The required cameras and sensors are already built into models including the 3 Series, 7 Series, X5, iX3 and iX4, and BMW can activate the feature over the air. The Verge says the system follows new European safety rules allowing automated driving moves on city streets. BMW says outside experts have road-tested it and confirmed it meets technical standards, with final government approval expected in early 2027.

The Verge also notes that safety researchers are increasingly worried about driver attention in Level 2 systems. It says drivers tend to over-rely on them and react slowly when they must take control. BMW stresses that drivers remain responsible for the vehicle. The Verge adds that some Tesla customers have successfully argued in court that Tesla bears some responsibility for crashes.
